claim: PP2A-B56 is a serine/threonine phosphatase complex that regulates sister chromatid cohesion during mitosis.
source: PP2A-B56 is a serine/threonine phosphatase complex that regulates several major mitotic processes, including sister chromatid cohesion, kinetochore-microtubule attachment and the spindle assembly checkpoint.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to prior work (Kitajima et al., 2006; Riedel et al., 2006; Tang et al., 2006) in the introduction.

claim: PP2A-B56 regulates kinetochore-microtubule attachment during mitosis.
source: PP2A-B56 is a serine/threonine phosphatase complex that regulates several major mitotic processes, including sister chromatid cohesion, kinetochore-microtubule attachment and the spindle assembly checkpoint.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to prior work (Foley et al., 2011; Kruse et al., 2013; Suijkerbuijk et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2013) in the introduction.

claim: PP2A-B56 regulates the spindle assembly checkpoint during mitosis.
source: PP2A-B56 is a serine/threonine phosphatase complex that regulates several major mitotic processes, including sister chromatid cohesion, kinetochore-microtubule attachment and the spindle assembly checkpoint.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to prior work (Espert et al., 2014; Nijenhuis et al., 2014) in the introduction.

claim: Different B56 isoforms localize to either the centromere or kinetochore.
source: We show here that these key functions are divided between different B56 isoforms that localise to either the centromere or kinetochore.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1a,b.

claim: B56γ and B56δ localize predominantly to kinetochores.
source: This revealed that while some B56 isoforms localise predominantly to the sister kinetochore pairs marked by Cenp-C (B56γ and δ), others localise mainly to the centromere defined by Sgo2 (B56α and ε), and one isoform displayed a mixed localisation pattern (B56β) (Figure 1a,b).
evidence: This is directly observed in immunofluorescence experiments shown in Figure 1a,b.

claim: B56α and B56ε localize mainly to the centromere.
source: This revealed that while some B56 isoforms localise predominantly to the sister kinetochore pairs marked by Cenp-C (B56γ and δ), others localise mainly to the centromere defined by Sgo2 (B56α and ε), and one isoform displayed a mixed localisation pattern (B56β) (Figure 1a,b).
evidence: This is directly observed in immunofluorescence experiments shown in Figure 1a,b.

claim: B56β displays a mixed localization pattern between centromere and kinetochore.
source: This revealed that while some B56 isoforms localise predominantly to the sister kinetochore pairs marked by Cenp-C (B56γ and δ), others localise mainly to the centromere defined by Sgo2 (B56α and ε), and one isoform displayed a mixed localisation pattern (B56β) (Figure 1a,b).
evidence: This is directly observed in immunofluorescence experiments shown in Figure 1a,b.

claim: Centromeric B56 isoforms rely on a specific interaction with Sgo2.
source: The centromeric isoforms rely on a specific interaction with Sgo2, whereas the kinetochore isoforms bind preferentially to BubR1 and other proteins containing an LxxIxE motif.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 2 showing Sgo2 depletion reduces centromeric B56α and by in-cell interaction assays.

claim: Kinetochore B56 isoforms bind preferentially to BubR1 and other proteins containing an LxxIxE motif.
source: The centromeric isoforms rely on a specific interaction with Sgo2, whereas the kinetochore isoforms bind preferentially to BubR1 and other proteins containing an LxxIxE motif.
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4 and localization studies in Figure 3.

claim: Sgo1 helps to anchor PP2A-B56 at both the centromere and kinetochore.
source: In addition to these selective binding partners, Sgo1 helps to anchor PP2A-B56 at both locations: it collaborates with BubR1 to maintain B56 at the kinetochore and it helps to preserve the Sgo2/B56 complex at the centromere.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2e showing Sgo1 depletion affects Sgo2-B56α localization and Figure 3g,h showing Sgo1 depletion reduces kinetochore B56γ.

claim: A small C-terminal loop in B56 regulates the key interactions and defines B56 localization.
source: A series of chimaeras were generated to map the critical region in B56 down to a small C-terminal loop that regulates the key interactions and defines B56 localisation.
evidence: This is supported by chimera experiments in Figure 5 showing that a 4-amino acid loop (EPVA vs TKHG) switches localization.

claim: PP2A is composed of a catalytic (C), scaffold (A) and regulatory (B) subunit.
source: Protein Phosphatase 2A (PP2A) is a major class of serine/threonine phosphatase that is composed of a catalytic (C), scaffold (A) and regulatory (B) subunit.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PP2A structure cited from Seshacharyulu et al., 2013.

claim: Substrate specificity of PP2A is mediated by the regulatory B subunits.
source: Substrate specificity is mediated by the regulatory B subunits, which can be subdivided into four structurally distinct families: B (B55), B' (B56), B' (PR72) and B'' (Striatin) (Seshacharyulu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Seshacharyulu et al., 2013.

claim: The B subunits can be subdivided into four structurally distinct families: B (B55), B' (B56), B'' (PR72) and B''' (Striatin).
source: Substrate specificity is mediated by the regulatory B subunits, which can be subdivided into four structurally distinct families: B (B55), B' (B56), B' (PR72) and B'' (Striatin) (Seshacharyulu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Seshacharyulu et al., 2013.

claim: In humans, the B subunits are encoded by a total of 15 separate genes which give rise to at least 26 different transcripts and splice variants.
source: In humans, the B subunits are encoded by a total of 15 separate genes which give rise to at least 26 different transcripts and splice variants; therefore, each of the four B subfamilies are composed of multiple different isoforms (Seshacharyulu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Seshacharyulu et al., 2013.

claim: B56 isoforms localize differently during mitosis.
source: Perhaps the best indirect evidence that they can comes from the observation that B56 isoforms localise differently during mitosis (Bastos et al., 2014; Nijenhuis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from prior work by Bastos et al., 2014 and Nijenhuis et al., 2014.

claim: PP2A activity is essential to regulate sister chromatid cohesion during prometaphase.
source: We addressed this problem by focussing on prometaphase, a stage in mitosis when PP2A activity is essential to regulate sister chromatid cohesion (Kitajima et al., 2006; Riedel et al., 2006; Tang et al., 2006), kinetochore-microtubule attachments (Foley et al., 2011; Kruse et al., 2013; Suijkerbuijk et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2013) and the spindle assembly checkpoint (Espert et al., 2014; Nijenhuis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from prior work (Kitajima et al., 2006; Riedel et al., 2006; Tang et al., 2006).

claim: PP2A activity is essential to regulate kinetochore-microtubule attachments during prometaphase.
source: We addressed this problem by focussing on prometaphase, a stage in mitosis when PP2A activity is essential to regulate sister chromatid cohesion (Kitajima et al., 2006; Riedel et al., 2006; Tang et al., 2006), kinetochore-microtubule attachments (Foley et al., 2011; Kruse et al., 2013; Suijkerbuijk et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2013) and the spindle assembly checkpoint (Espert et al., 2014; Nijenhuis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from prior work (Foley et al., 2011; Kruse et al., 2013; Suijkerbuijk et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2013).

claim: PP2A activity is essential to regulate the spindle assembly checkpoint during prometaphase.
source: We addressed this problem by focussing on prometaphase, a stage in mitosis when PP2A activity is essential to regulate sister chromatid cohesion (Kitajima et al., 2006; Riedel et al., 2006; Tang et al., 2006), kinetochore-microtubule attachments (Foley et al., 2011; Kruse et al., 2013; Suijkerbuijk et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2013) and the spindle assembly checkpoint (Espert et al., 2014; Nijenhuis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from prior work (Espert et al., 2014; Nijenhuis et al., 2014).

claim: Aurora B is critical for destabilizing incorrectly attached microtubules.
source: The kinase Aurora B is critical for both processes because it phosphorylates the kinetochore-microtubule interface to destabilise incorrectly attached microtubules and it reinforces the SAC, in part by antagonising Knl1-PP1, a kinetochore phosphatase complex needed for SAC silencing (Saurin, 2018).
evidence: This is cited from Saurin, 2018.

claim: Aurora B reinforces the SAC by antagonizing Knl1-PP1.
source: The kinase Aurora B is critical for both processes because it phosphorylates the kinetochore-microtubule interface to destabilise incorrectly attached microtubules and it reinforces the SAC, in part by antagonising Knl1-PP1, a kinetochore phosphatase complex needed for SAC silencing (Saurin, 2018).
evidence: This is cited from Saurin, 2018.

claim: PP2A-B56 localizes to the Knl1 complex at the outer kinetochore by binding directly to BubR1.
source: These two principal functions of Aurora B are antagonised by PP2A-B56, which localises to the Knl1 complex at the outer kinetochore by binding directly to BubR1 (Foley et al., 2011; Kruse et al., 2013; Suijkerbuijk et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from prior work (Foley et al., 2011; Kruse et al., 2013; Suijkerbuijk et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2013).

claim: The B56 subunit interacts with a phosphorylated LxxIxE motif within the KARD of BubR1.
source: This interaction is mediated by the B56 subunit, which interacts with a phosphorylated LxxIxE motif within the kinetochore attachment regulatory domain (KARD) of BubR1 (Wang et al., 2016a; Wang et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is cited from Wang et al., 2016a and Wang et al., 2016b.

claim: PP2A-B56 localizes to the centromere by binding to shugoshin 1 and 2 (Sgo1/Sgo2).
source: As well as localising to the outer kinetochore, PP2A-B56 also localises to the centromere by binding to shugoshin 1 and 2 (Sgo1/Sgo2) (Kitajima et al., 2006; Riedel et al., 2006; Rivera et al., 2012; Tang et al., 2006; Tanno et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from prior work (Kitajima et al., 2006; Riedel et al., 2006; Rivera et al., 2012; Tang et al., 2006; Tanno et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2009).

claim: The crystal structure of Sgo1 bound to PP2A-B56 reveals a bipartite interaction between Sgo1 and the regulatory and catalytic subunits of the PP2A-B56 complex.
source: The crystal structure of Sgo1 bound to PP2A-B56 has been solved to reveal a bipartite interaction between Sgo1 and the regulatory and catalytic subunits of the PP2A-B56 complex (Xu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from Xu et al., 2009.

claim: Centromere-localized PP2A-B56 counteracts kinases such as Aurora B to preserve cohesin at the centromere.
source: This interaction is thought to allow centromere-localised PP2A-B56 to counteract various kinases, such as Aurora B, which remove cohesin rings from chromosome arms during early mitosis in higher eukaryotes (Marston, 2015). The result is that cohesin is specifically preserved at the centromere where it is needed to resist the pulling forces exerted by microtubules.
evidence: This is cited from Marston, 2015.

claim: PP2A-B56 balances the net level of Aurora B activation at the centromere.
source: As well as preserving cohesion at the centromere, PP2A-B56 is also thought to balance the net level of Aurora B activation in this region (Meppelink et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Meppelink et al., 2015.

claim: In human cells, B56 isoforms are encoded by five separate genes (B56α, β, γ, δ and ε).
source: In human cells, B56 isoforms are encoded by five separate genes (B56α, β, γ, δ and ε).
evidence: This is established knowledge about human B56 genes.

claim: The interaction interfaces involved in BubR1 and Sgo1 binding are extremely well conserved between all B56 isoforms.
source: The interaction interfaces involved in BubR1 and Sgo1 binding are extremely well conserved between all of these B56 isoforms (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by sequence alignment in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: BubR1 and Sgo1 appear to display no specificity for individual B56 isoforms.
source: This explains why BubR1 and Sgo1 appear to display no specificity for individual B56 isoforms (Kitajima et al., 2006; Kruse et al., 2013; Riedel et al., 2006; Xu et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2009), and why these isoforms have been proposed to function redundantly at kinetochores during mitosis (Foley et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from prior work (Kitajima et al., 2006; Kruse et al., 2013; Riedel et al., 2006; Xu et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2009).

claim: B56 isoforms have been proposed to function redundantly at kinetochores during mitosis.
source: This explains why BubR1 and Sgo1 appear to display no specificity for individual B56 isoforms (Kitajima et al., 2006; Kruse et al., 2013; Riedel et al., 2006; Xu et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2009), and why these isoforms have been proposed to function redundantly at kinetochores during mitosis (Foley et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from Foley et al., 2011.

claim: Individual B56 isoforms localize differentially to either the kinetochore or centromere in human cells.
source: However, one crucial observation throws doubt over this issue of redundancy: individual B56 isoforms localise differentially to either the kinetochore or centromere in human cells (Meppelink et al., 2015; Nijenhuis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Meppelink et al., 2015 and Nijenhuis et al., 2014.

claim: Only the centromere-localized B56α can support proper centromeric cohesion.
source: In agreement with our differential localisation data, only the centromere-localised B56α was able to support proper centromeric cohesion (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is shown by chromosome spread analysis in Figure 1c.

claim: Sister chromatid cohesion can be supported by B56α but not by B56γ.
source: Therefore, sister chromatid cohesion can be supported by a B56 isoform that localises primarily to the centromere (B56α), but not by one that localises to the kinetochore (B56γ).
evidence: This is concluded from the data in Figure 1c showing B56γ cannot rescue cohesion defects.

claim: The SAC is activated at kinetochores by the phosphorylation of 'MELT' repeats on Knl1 by the kinase Mps1.
source: The SAC is activated at kinetochores by the phosphorylation of 'MELT' repeats on Knl1 by the kinase Mps1 (London et al., 2012; Shepperd et al., 2012; Yamagishi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from prior work (London et al., 2012; Shepperd et al., 2012; Yamagishi et al., 2012).

claim: Removal of B56 from kinetochores prevents Knl1-MELT dephosphorylation.
source: PP2A-B56 antagonises this process, as evidenced by the fact that removal of B56 from kinetochores prevents Knl1-MELT dephosphorylation and delays mitotic exit following Mps1 inhibition in nocodazole (Espert et al., 2014; Nijenhuis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Espert et al., 2014 and Nijenhuis et al., 2014.

claim: Removal of B56 from kinetochores delays mitotic exit following Mps1 inhibition in nocodazole.
source: PP2A-B56 antagonises this process, as evidenced by the fact that removal of B56 from kinetochores prevents Knl1-MELT dephosphorylation and delays mitotic exit following Mps1 inhibition in nocodazole (Espert et al., 2014; Nijenhuis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Espert et al., 2014 and Nijenhuis et al., 2014.

claim: Simultaneous depletion of all B56 isoforms enhances basal Knl1-MELT phosphorylation in nocodazole.
source: As expected, simultaneous depletion of all B56 isoforms enhanced basal Knl1-MELT phosphorylation in nocodazole, delayed MELT dephosphorylation upon Mps1 inhibition with AZ-3146 (Hewitt et al., 2010), and prevented mitotic exit under identical conditions (Figure 1d–f).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 1d-f.

claim: Depletion of all B56 isoforms delays MELT dephosphorylation upon Mps1 inhibition.
source: As expected, simultaneous depletion of all B56 isoforms enhanced basal Knl1-MELT phosphorylation in nocodazole, delayed MELT dephosphorylation upon Mps1 inhibition with AZ-3146 (Hewitt et al., 2010), and prevented mitotic exit under identical conditions (Figure 1d–f).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 1d-f.

claim: Depletion of all B56 isoforms prevents mitotic exit following Mps1 inhibition.
source: As expected, simultaneous depletion of all B56 isoforms enhanced basal Knl1-MELT phosphorylation in nocodazole, delayed MELT dephosphorylation upon Mps1 inhibition with AZ-3146 (Hewitt et al., 2010), and prevented mitotic exit under identical conditions (Figure 1d–f).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 1d-f.

claim: Endogenous B56γ can rescue SAC silencing defects caused by depletion of all B56 isoforms.
source: Importantly, these effects were all rescued when endogenous B56γ was preserved, but not if only B56α remained (Figure 1d–f).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 1d-f.

claim: Endogenous B56α cannot rescue SAC silencing defects caused by depletion of all B56 isoforms.
source: Importantly, these effects were all rescued when endogenous B56γ was preserved, but not if only B56α remained (Figure 1d–f).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 1d-f.

claim: Kinetochore PP2A-B56 is needed to antagonize Aurora B and allow initial kinetochore-microtubule attachment to form.
source: Kinetochore PP2A-B56 also has well-established roles in chromosome alignment where it is needed to antagonise Aurora B and allow initial kinetochore-microtubule attachment to form (Foley et al., 2011; Kruse et al., 2013; Suijkerbuijk et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from prior work (Foley et al., 2011; Kruse et al., 2013; Suijkerbuijk et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2013).

claim: Knockdown of all B56 isoforms produces severe defects in chromosome alignment.
source: Knockdown of all B56 isoforms produced severe defects in chromosome alignment, as expected, and these effects could be rescued by preserving B56γ, but not B56α (Figure 1g).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 1g.

claim: B56γ can rescue chromosome alignment defects caused by depletion of all B56 isoforms.
source: Knockdown of all B56 isoforms produced severe defects in chromosome alignment, as expected, and these effects could be rescued by preserving B56γ, but not B56α (Figure 1g).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 1g.

claim: B56α cannot rescue chromosome alignment defects caused by depletion of all B56 isoforms.
source: Knockdown of all B56 isoforms produced severe defects in chromosome alignment, as expected, and these effects could be rescued by preserving B56γ, but not B56α (Figure 1g).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 1g.

claim: Only the kinetochore-localized B56γ, and not the centromeric B56α, can support SAC silencing and chromosome alignment in human cells.
source: In summary, only the kinetochore-localised B56γ, and not the centromeric B56α, can support SAC silencing and chromosome alignment in human cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the data in Figure 1d-g.

claim: Overexpression of GFP-B56α can rescue kinetochore-microtubule attachment defects following the depletion of all PP2A-B56 isoforms in human cells.
source: Overexpression of GFP-B56α has previously been shown to rescue kinetochore-microtubule attachment defects following the depletion of all PP2A-B56 isoforms in human cells (Foley et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from Foley et al., 2011.

claim: Exogenous YFP-B56α and YFP-B56γ can both rescue MELT dephosphorylation, SAC silencing and chromosome alignment when overexpressed.
source: Under these conditions, both exogenous B56 isoforms were able to rescue MELT dephosphorylation, SAC silencing and chromosome alignment (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Exogenous YFP-B56α is highly overexpressed compared to endogenous YFP-B56α.
source: The ability of exogenous YFP-B56α to support kinetochore functions can be explained by the fact that it is highly overexpressed, which leads to elevated centromere and kinetochore levels in comparison to the endogenous YFP-B56α situation (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: B56α acts primarily at the centromere, but it can still function at the kinetochore when overexpressed.
source: We therefore conclude B56α acts primarily at the centromere, but it can still function at the kinetochore when overexpressed.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of endogenous and overexpressed B56α data.

claim: Under endogenous conditions, PP2A-B56 isoforms localize differentially to the centromere or kinetochore where they carry out specific roles in sister chromatid cohesion, SAC silencing and chromosomal alignment.
source: In summary, under endogenous conditions, PP2A-B56 isoforms localise differentially to the centromere or kinetochore where they carry out specific roles in sister chromatid cohesion, SAC silencing and chromosomal alignment.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the data in Figure 1.

claim: Sgo1 and Sgo2 can both bind to PP2A-B56 at the centromere.
source: At the centromere, Sgo1 and Sgo2 can both bind to PP2A-B56 (Rivera et al., 2012; Tanno et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2009), but Sgo1 is considered the primary receptor because it is more important than Sgo2 for protecting cohesion in mitosis (Huang et al., 2007; Kitajima et al., 2005; Kitajima et al., 2006; Llano et al., 2008; McGuinness et al., 2005; Rivera et al., 2012; Tang et al., 2006; Tanno et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from prior work (Rivera et al., 2012; Tanno et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2009).

claim: Sgo1 is considered the primary receptor for PP2A-B56 at centromeres because it is more important than Sgo2 for protecting cohesion in mitosis.
source: At the centromere, Sgo1 and Sgo2 can both bind to PP2A-B56 (Rivera et al., 2012; Tanno et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2009), but Sgo1 is considered the primary receptor because it is more important than Sgo2 for protecting cohesion in mitosis (Huang et al., 2007; Kitajima et al., 2005; Kitajima et al., 2006; Llano et al., 2008; McGuinness et al., 2005; Rivera et al., 2012; Tang et al., 2006; Tanno et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from prior work (Huang et al., 2007; Kitajima et al., 2005; Kitajima et al., 2006; Llano et al., 2008; McGuinness et al., 2005; Rivera et al., 2012; Tang et al., 2006; Tanno et al., 2010).

claim: Sgo2 is more important than Sgo1 for centromeric PP2A-B56 recruitment.
source: Furthermore, although Sgo1 has been implicated in PP2A-B56 recruitment to centromeres (Liu et al., 2013a; Liu et al., 2013b; Nishiyama et al., 2013; Tang et al., 2006), the only study that has directly compared the contribution of Sgo1 and Sgo2 to centromeric PP2A-B56 recruitment, has concluded that Sgo2 is more important (Kitajima et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited from Kitajima et al., 2006.

claim: Depletion of Sgo2, but not Sgo1, causes a significant reduction in B56α levels at the centromere.
source: Depletion of Sgo2, but not Sgo1, caused a significant reduction in B56α levels at the centromere (Figure 2a–d).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 2a-d.

claim: Sgo1 depletion shifts B56α localization towards the kinetochore.
source: It is important to note that the quantification in Figure 2b and d cannot distinguish between kinetochore and centromere localisation, and whilst Sgo1 depletion did not reduce B56, it did appear to shift its localisation towards the kinetochore (see zoom panel in Figure 2c), an effect that has previously been seen by others (Meppelink et al., 2015).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 2c and cited from Meppelink et al., 2015.

claim: Sgo1 depletion causes Sgo2 and B56α to spread out from the centromere towards the kinetochore.
source: Line plots analysis, which can quantify localisation across the centromere-kinetochore axis, demonstrates that Sgo1 depletion caused Sgo2 and B56α to spread out from the centromere towards the kinetochore (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is shown by line plot analysis in Figure 2e.

claim: Combined Sgo1 and Sgo2 depletion completely removes B56α from kinetochores and centromeres.
source: This is due to inefficient anchoring of Sgo2 at centromeres because combined Sgo1 and Sgo2 depletion completely removed B56α from kinetochores and centromeres (Figure 2f,g).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 2f,g.

claim: Sgo2 is the primary centromeric receptor for PP2A-B56 during mitosis.
source: We therefore conclude that, as suggested previously by others (Kitajima et al., 2006), Sgo2 is the primary centromeric receptor for PP2A-B56 during mitosis.
evidence: This is concluded from the data in Figure 2 and cited from Kitajima et al., 2006.

claim: Sgo1 contributes to centromeric B56 localization primarily by helping to anchor the Sgo2-B56 complex at the centromere.
source: However, Sgo1 also contributes to centromeric B56 localisation primarily by helping to anchor the Sgo2-B56 complex at the centromere, perhaps by bridging an interaction with cohesin rings or by helping to preserve centromeric cohesion (Hara et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is inferred from the data in Figure 2 and cited from Hara et al., 2014 and Liu et al., 2013b.

claim: CB-Sgo2 is only able to recruit additional B56α but not B56γ.
source: Whereas CB-Sgo1 was able to localise additional B56α and B56γ to the inner kinetochore (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), CB-Sgo2 was only able to recruit additional B56α (Figure 2h–k).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 2h-k.

claim: Only B56α, and not B56γ, is able to co-recruit endogenous Sgo2 to chromosome 7.
source: This assay confirmed that only B56α, and not B56γ, was able to co-recruit endogenous Sgo2 to this region (Figure 2l,m).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 2l,m using the dCas9-DARPin system.

claim: Sgo2 being the primary centromeric receptor for B56 explains why only a subset of B56 isoforms localize to the centromere.
source: Considering Sgo2 is the primary centromeric receptor for B56 (Figure 2a,b) (Kitajima et al., 2006), this provides an explanation for why only a subset of B56 isoforms localise to the centromere.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing Sgo2 selectivity for B56α.

claim: BubR1 depletion reduces but does not completely remove B56γ from kinetochores/centromere.
source: In agreement with this hypothesis, BubR1 depletion or mutation of the LxxIxE binding pocket in B56γ (B56γH187A) reduced but did not completely remove B56γ from kinetochores/centromere (Figure 3a–d).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 3a-d.

claim: Mutation of the LxxIxE binding pocket in B56γ (B56γH187A) reduces but does not completely remove B56γ from kinetochores/centromere.
source: In agreement with this hypothesis, BubR1 depletion or mutation of the LxxIxE binding pocket in B56γ (B56γH187A) reduced but did not completely remove B56γ from kinetochores/centromere (Figure 3a–d).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 3a-d.

claim: The remaining B56γ after BubR1 depletion or H187A mutation spreads out between the kinetochore and centromere.
source: Interestingly, the remaining B56γ in these situations spreads out between the kinetochore and centromere (Figure 3e,f), which implies that B56γ uses additional interactions to be maintained at this region.
evidence: This is shown by line plot analysis in Figure 3e,f.

claim: B56γ uses additional interactions beyond BubR1 to be maintained at the kinetochore/centromere region.
source: Interestingly, the remaining B56γ in these situations spreads out between the kinetochore and centromere (Figure 3e,f), which implies that B56γ uses additional interactions to be maintained at this region.
evidence: This is inferred from the data in Figure 3e,f.

claim: Knl1 depletion completely abolishes B56γ recruitment to kinetochores.
source: A targeted siRNA screen identified critical roles for Knl1 and Bub1, which, when depleted, completely abolished B56γ recruitment to kinetochores (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c–f).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c-f.

claim: Bub1 depletion completely abolishes B56γ recruitment to kinetochores.
source: A targeted siRNA screen identified critical roles for Knl1 and Bub1, which, when depleted, completely abolished B56γ recruitment to kinetochores (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c–f).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c-f.

claim: Bub1 phosphorylates histone-H2A to localize Sgo1 to histone tails adjacent to the kinetochore.
source: However, in addition to this, Bub1 also phosphorylates histone-H2A to localise Sgo1 to histone tails that are adjacent to the kinetochore (Baron et al., 2016; Kawashima et al., 2010; Kitajima et al., 2005; Liu et al., 2013a; Tang et al., 2004; Yamagishi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from prior work (Baron et al., 2016; Kawashima et al., 2010; Kitajima et al., 2005; Liu et al., 2013a; Tang et al., 2004; Yamagishi et al., 2010).

claim: Sgo1 depletion reduces B56γWT at kinetochores and completely removes B56γH187A.
source: Sgo1 depletion reduced B56γWT at kinetochores and completely removed B56γH187A (Figure 3g,h).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 3g,h.

claim: Sgo2 depletion has no effect on B56γ kinetochore localization.
source: Moreover, this was specific for Sgo1, because Sgo2 depletion had no effect (Figure 3—figure supplement 1g,h).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1g,h.

claim: B56γΔSgo1 is defective in binding CB-Sgo1 in vivo.
source: To test whether this was due to direct binding to Sgo1, we generated a B56γ Sgo1-binding mutant (B56γΔSgo1), which we confirmed was defective in binding CB-Sgo1 in vivo (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The B56γΔSgo1 mutation reduces the recruitment of B56γWT to kinetochores and completely abolishes the recruitment of B56γH187A.
source: This mutation reduced the recruitment of B56γWT to kinetochores and completely abolished the recruitment of B56γH187A (Figure 3i,j), in a manner that was similar to the effect of Sgo1 depletion (Figure 3g,h).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 3i,j.

claim: Bub1 establishes two separate arms that cooperate to recruit B56γ to kinetochores: direct binding to BubR1 and phosphorylation of Histone-H2A to recruit Sgo1.
source: This demonstrates that Bub1 establishes two separate arms that cooperate to recruit B56γ to kinetochores: it binds directly to BubR1, which interacts via its LxxIxE motif with B56γ, and it phosphorylates Histone-H2A to recruit Sgo1, which additionally helps to anchor B56γ at kinetochores.
evidence: This is concluded from the data in Figure 3.

claim: BubR1 binds preferentially to B56γ over B56α in nocodazole-arrested cells.
source: Immunoprecipitations of equal amounts of B56α and B56γ from nocodazole-arrested cells demonstrated that BubR1 bound preferentially to B56γ (Figure 4a,b).
evidence: This is shown by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4a,b.

claim: LxxIxE binding is generally reduced in B56α immunoprecipitates compared to B56γ.
source: Moreover, a panel of antibodies against other LxxIxE containing proteins (Hertz et al., 2016), demonstrated that LxxIxE binding was generally reduced in B56α immunoprecipitates (Figure 4a,b).
evidence: This is shown by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4a,b.

claim: B56γ displays slightly higher affinities for some LxxIxE containing peptides in vitro.
source: B56γ has been shown to display slightly higher affinities for some LxxIxE containing peptides in vitro (Wu et al., 2017), which, in principle, could allow this isoform to outcompete B56α for binding.
evidence: This is cited from Wu et al., 2017.

claim: A simple competition model is unlikely to explain differential kinetochore localization of B56 isoforms.
source: However, a simple competition model is unlikely to explain differential kinetochore localisation, since we observe no change in B56α localisation when all other B56 isoforms are present or knocked down (Figure 4c,d).
evidence: This is inferred from the data in Figure 4c,d.

claim: Binding to LxxIxE motifs is specifically perturbed in PP2A-B56α complexes during prometaphase.
source: Instead, we favour the hypothesis that binding to LxxIxE motifs is specifically perturbed in PP2A-B56α complexes during prometaphase.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the data showing differential LxxIxE binding.

claim: B56γ localization switches from kinetochores to centromeres in chimera 4.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis demonstrated that B56γ localisation switched from kinetochores to centromeres in chimaera 4 (Figure 5b,c).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 5b,c.

claim: The region between chimaeras 3 and 4 is sufficient to switch localization to the centromere when transferred into B56γ.
source: Furthermore, this region alone (i.e. the region that is different between chimaeras 3 and 4) is sufficient to switch localisation to the centromere when transferred into B56γ, and the corresponding region in B56γ can induce localisation to the kinetochore if transplanted into B56α (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The corresponding region in B56γ can induce localization to the kinetochore if transplanted into B56α.
source: Furthermore, this region alone (i.e. the region that is different between chimaeras 3 and 4) is sufficient to switch localisation to the centromere when transferred into B56γ, and the corresponding region in B56γ can induce localisation to the kinetochore if transplanted into B56α (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Amino acids 405-425 in B56α control centromere/kinetochore localization.
source: We generated four additional chimaeras to narrow down this region even further to amino acids 405–425 in B56α, which contains an α-helix and a small loop that juxtaposes the catalytic domain in the PP2A-B56γ complex (Figure 5d–f) (Xu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 5d-f and cited from Xu et al., 2006.

claim: Switching four amino acids within the EPVA loop in B56α to the corresponding residues in B56γ (B56αTKHG) is sufficient to relocalize B56α from centromeres to kinetochores.
source: Importantly, switching just four amino acids within this loop in B56α to the corresponding residues in B56γ (B56αTKHG) was sufficient to relocalise B56α from centromeres to kinetochores (Figure 5g–i).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 5g-i.

claim: B56αTKHG remains functional and holoenzyme assembly is unperturbed.
source: Furthermore, the B56αTKHG remained functional and holoenzyme assembly was unperturbed (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: A small C-terminal loop in B56 defines whether B56 localizes to centromeres, via Sgo2, or to kinetochores, via an LxxIxE interaction with BubR1.
source: In summary, a small C-terminal loop in B56 defines whether B56 localises to centromeres, via Sgo2, or to kinetochores, via an LxxIxE interaction with BubR1.
evidence: This is concluded from the chimera experiments in Figure 5.

claim: B56αTKHG is not efficiently recruited to the centromere by CB-Sgo2.
source: In-cell interaction assays demonstrated that B56αTKHG, in contrast to B56αWT, was not efficiently recruited to the centromere by CB-Sgo2 (Figure 6a,b), and was unable to co-recruit endogenous Sgo2 to the repeat region on chromosome 7, when re-localised there using dCas9-DARPin (Figure 6c,d).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 6a,b.

claim: B56αTKHG is unable to co-recruit endogenous Sgo2 to the repeat region on chromosome 7.
source: In-cell interaction assays demonstrated that B56αTKHG, in contrast to B56αWT, was not efficiently recruited to the centromere by CB-Sgo2 (Figure 6a,b), and was unable to co-recruit endogenous Sgo2 to the repeat region on chromosome 7, when re-localised there using dCas9-DARPin (Figure 6c,d).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 6c,d.

claim: YFP-B56αTKHG shows an enhanced ability to bind LxxIxE containing proteins, particularly BubR1, following immunoprecipitation from nocodazole-arrested cells.
source: Furthermore, in addition to these effects on Sgo2 interaction, the YFP-B56αTKHG mutant showed an enhanced ability to bind LxxIxE containing proteins and, in particular, BubR1, following immunoprecipitation from nocodazole-arrested cells (Figure 6e,f).
evidence: This is shown by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6e,f.

claim: The small EPVA loop in B56α is necessary for the interaction with Sgo2 and the centromere.
source: Therefore, we conclude that the small EPVA loop in B56α is necessary for the interaction with Sgo2 and the centromere and, in addition, it is also required to fully repress binding to LxxIxE motifs and the kinetochore.
evidence: This is concluded from the data in Figure 6.

claim: The EPVA loop in B56α is required to fully repress binding to LxxIxE motifs and the kinetochore.
source: Therefore, we conclude that the small EPVA loop in B56α is necessary for the interaction with Sgo2 and the centromere and, in addition, it is also required to fully repress binding to LxxIxE motifs and the kinetochore.
evidence: This is concluded from the data in Figure 6.

claim: The EPVA loop is not sufficient to induce centromere localization when transplanted alone into B56γ.
source: Importantly, this loop is not sufficient to induce either of these effects when transplanted alone into B56γ, because B56γEPVA is not lost from the kinetochore or gained at the centromere (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a.

claim: A region immediately C-terminal to the EPVA (amino acids 414-453 in B56α) is required to induce centromere binding.
source: Instead, a region immediately C-terminal to the EPVA (amino acids 414–453 in B56α) is also required to induce centromere binding, and a small helix N-terminal to the EPVA (amino acids 374–386 in B56α) is needed to repress kinetochore binding (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b.

claim: A small helix N-terminal to the EPVA (amino acids 374-386 in B56α) is needed to repress kinetochore binding.
source: Instead, a region immediately C-terminal to the EPVA (amino acids 414–453 in B56α) is also required to induce centromere binding, and a small helix N-terminal to the EPVA (amino acids 374–386 in B56α) is needed to repress kinetochore binding (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The regions that define centromere and kinetochore localization overlap at the EPVA loop but have different distal requirements.
source: Therefore, although the regions that define centromere and kinetochore localisation overlap at the EPVA loop, they have different distal requirements that demonstrates that they are not identical (Figure 6g).
evidence: This is concluded from the data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b and summarized in Figure 6g.

claim: Differential B56 isoform localization has previously been observed in interphase.
source: Differential B56 isoform localisation has previously been observed in interphase (McCright et al., 1996) and during the later stages of mitosis (Bastos et al., 2014), which implies that B56 isoforms may have evolved to carry out specific functions, at least in part, by targeting PP2A to distinct subcellular compartments.
evidence: This is cited from McCright et al., 1996.

claim: Differential B56 isoform localization has been observed during the later stages of mitosis.
source: Differential B56 isoform localisation has previously been observed in interphase (McCright et al., 1996) and during the later stages of mitosis (Bastos et al., 2014), which implies that B56 isoforms may have evolved to carry out specific functions, at least in part, by targeting PP2A to distinct subcellular compartments.
evidence: This is cited from Bastos et al., 2014.

claim: B56 isoforms may have evolved to carry out specific functions by targeting PP2A to distinct subcellular compartments.
source: Differential B56 isoform localisation has previously been observed in interphase (McCright et al., 1996) and during the later stages of mitosis (Bastos et al., 2014), which implies that B56 isoforms may have evolved to carry out specific functions, at least in part, by targeting PP2A to distinct subcellular compartments.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of differential localization.

claim: The centromeric isoform B56α binds preferentially to Sgo2 via a C-terminal stretch between amino acids 405 and 453.
source: The centromeric isoform B56α binds preferentially to Sgo2 via a C-terminal stretch that lies between amino acids 405 and 453 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is concluded from the data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: A key loop within the C-terminal region juxtaposes the catalytic domain and contains an important EPVA signature that is critical for Sgo2 binding.
source: A key loop within this region juxtaposes the catalytic domain and contains an important EPVA signature that is critical for Sgo2 binding and is unique to B56α and B56ε.
evidence: This is concluded from the chimera and mutation experiments.

claim: The EPVA sequence is unique to B56α and B56ε.
source: A key loop within this region juxtaposes the catalytic domain and contains an important EPVA signature that is critical for Sgo2 binding and is unique to B56α and B56ε.
evidence: This is observed from sequence analysis shown in Figure 5g.

claim: The EPVA sequence is conserved in Xenopus B56ε.
source: This sequence is also conserved in Xenopus B56ε, which has previously been shown to selectively bind to Sgo2, when compared to B56γ (Rivera et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Rivera et al., 2012.

claim: A subset of B56 isoforms (B56α and ε) utilize unique motifs to interact with Sgo2 and the centromere during mitosis.
source: We therefore propose that a subset of B56 isoforms (B56α and ε) utilize unique motifs to interact with Sgo2 and the centromere during mitosis.
evidence: This is proposed based on the data showing EPVA is unique to B56α and ε and is critical for Sgo2 binding.

claim: Sgo1 can compete with the cohesin release factor WAPL for cohesin binding, thereby protecting cohesion independently of PP2A.
source: Firstly, it is important to note that Sgo1 can compete with the cohesin release factor, WAPL, for cohesin binding (Hara et al., 2014), thereby protecting cohesion independently of PP2A.
evidence: This is cited from Hara et al., 2014.

claim: Sgo1 could help cells to tolerate the loss of Sgo2 because Sgo2 depletion does not fully remove PP2A-B56 from the centromere.
source: In addition, Sgo1 could help cells to tolerate the loss of Sgo2, because Sgo2 depletion does not fully remove PP2A-B56 from the centromere, and the pool that remains under these conditions is dependent on Sgo1 (Figure 2a–g).
evidence: This is inferred from the data in Figure 2a-g.

claim: Sgo1 is needed to preserve Sgo2-PP2A-B56 at the centromere.
source: Finally, Sgo1 is needed to preserve Sgo2-PP2A-B56 at the centromere (Figure 2e) and it can also bind directly to the SA2–Scc1 complex (Hara et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2013b; Tanno et al., 2010).
evidence: This is shown by data in Figure 2e.

claim: Sgo1 can bind directly to the SA2-Scc1 complex.
source: Finally, Sgo1 is needed to preserve Sgo2-PP2A-B56 at the centromere (Figure 2e) and it can also bind directly to the SA2–Scc1 complex (Hara et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2013b; Tanno et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Hara et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2013b; Tanno et al., 2010.

claim: Sgo1 may help to position Sgo2-PP2A-B56 so that it can dephosphorylate nearby residues within the cohesin complex.
source: Therefore, perhaps Sgo1 also helps to position Sgo2-PP2A-B56 so that it can dephosphorylate nearby residues within the cohesin complex.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known interactions.

claim: The LxxIxE binding pocket is completely conserved in all B56 isoforms.
source: Although the LxxIxE binding pocket is completely conserved in all B56 isoforms (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), we observe a striking preference in the binding of B56γ over B56α to many LxxIxE containing proteins during prometaphase (Figure 4).
evidence: This is shown by sequence alignment in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is a striking preference in the binding of B56γ over B56α to many LxxIxE containing proteins during prometaphase.
source: Although the LxxIxE binding pocket is completely conserved in all B56 isoforms (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), we observe a striking preference in the binding of B56γ over B56α to many LxxIxE containing proteins during prometaphase (Figure 4).
evidence: This is shown by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4.

claim: Binding between LxxIxE motifs and B56α is repressed during prometaphase.
source: We hypothesise that this is due to repressed binding between LxxIxE motifs and B56α during prometaphase, because LxxIxE binding (Figure 6e,f) and kinetochore accumulation (Figure 5h,j) can both be enhanced by mutation of the EPVA loop in B56α (B56αTKHG).
evidence: This is hypothesized based on the data in Figure 6e,f and Figure 5h,j.

claim: Sgo2 interaction is unlikely to obscure the LxxIxE binding pocket in B56α.
source: Considering that this region also controls Sgo2 and centromere binding, a simple explanation could be that Sgo2 interaction obscures the LxxIxE binding pocket. However, this appears unlikely for four reasons: 1) Sgo2 depletion does not relocalise B56α to kinetochores (Figure 2a,b), 2) Sgo2 depletion does not enhance the ability of B56α to bind to BubR1 or other LxxIxE motifs during mitosis (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), 3) centromere and kinetochore binding can occur together in certain B56α-γ chimaeras (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b), and 4) the regions that define each of these localisations do not fully overlap (Figure 6g).
evidence: This is concluded from multiple lines of evidence in Figures 2, 6.

claim: Another interacting partner or a tail region within a PP2A-B56 subunit might obscure or modify the conformation of the LxxIxE binding pocket in PP2A-B56α complexes.
source: If not Sgo2, then what could limit the kinetochore accumulation of B56α? We speculate that another interacting partner, or alternatively a tail region within a PP2A-B56 subunit, might obscure or modify the conformation of the LxxIxE binding pocket in PP2A-B56α complexes.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Sgo1 contributes to the B56γ signal observed at the kinetochore.
source: An important additional finding of this work is that Sgo1 contributes to the B56γ signal observed at the kinetochore (Figure 3g–j).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 3g-j.

claim: Sgo1's contribution to kinetochore B56γ likely requires Sgo1 to be bound to histone tails.
source: This likely requires Sgo1 to be bound to histone tails, because it also depends on Bub1, the kinase that phosphorylates histone H2A to recruit Sgo1 (Baron et al., 2016; Kawashima et al., 2010; Kitajima et al., 2005; Liu et al., 2013a; Tang et al., 2004; Yamagishi et al., 2010) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and cited from prior work.

claim: The interfaces between BubR1-B56 and Sgo1-PP2A-B56 do not appear to be overlapping based on current structural data.
source: The interfaces between BubR1-B56 and Sgo1-PP2A-B56 do not appear to be overlapping, at least based on current structural data (Wang et al., 2016a; Wang et al., 2016b; Xu et al., 2009), which implies that Knl1-bound BubR1-B56 could potentially be anchored towards histone tails by Sgo1.
evidence: This is inferred from structural data cited from Wang et al., 2016a; Wang et al., 2016b; Xu et al., 2009.

claim: Knl1-bound BubR1-B56 could potentially be anchored towards histone tails by Sgo1.
source: The interfaces between BubR1-B56 and Sgo1-PP2A-B56 do not appear to be overlapping, at least based on current structural data (Wang et al., 2016a; Wang et al., 2016b; Xu et al., 2009), which implies that Knl1-bound BubR1-B56 could potentially be anchored towards histone tails by Sgo1.
evidence: This is speculation based on structural considerations.

claim: This is the first time that sub-functionalization has been demonstrated between isoforms of the same B family.
source: This is the first time that such sub-functionalisation has been demonstrated between isoforms of the same B family.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: The use of different B56 isoforms may allow PP2A catalytic activity to be regulated differently in specific subcellular compartments.
source: One possibility is that the use of different B56 isoforms allows PP2A catalytic activity to be regulated differently in specific subcellular compartments: for example, by enabling interactions or post-translational modifications that are specific for the B56 subunits.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of isoform-specific localization.

claim: Protein inhibitors of PP2A-B56 have been shown to function specifically at the centromere (SET) and at the kinetochore (BOD1).
source: In this respect, protein inhibitors of PP2A-B56 have been shown to function specifically at the centromere (SET (Chambon et al., 2013)) and at the kinetochore (BOD1 (Porter et al., 2013)); therefore, it would be interesting to test whether these inhibitors display selectivity for certain PP2A-B56 isoforms.
evidence: This is cited from Chambon et al., 2013 and Porter et al., 2013.

claim: The recent development of selective inhibitors of related PP1 regulatory isoforms to combat neurodegenerative diseases provides proof-of-concept that successful targeting of specific serine/threonine phosphatase isoforms is both achievable and therapeutically valuable.
source: The recent development of selective inhibitors of related PP1 regulatory isoforms to combat neurodegenerative diseases (Das et al., 2015; Krzyzosiak et al., 2018), provides a proof-of-concept that successful targeting of specific serine/threonine phosphatase isoforms is both achievable and therapeutically valuable.
evidence: This is cited from Das et al., 2015 and Krzyzosiak et al., 2018.
